1:
Chrysostom reads the opening as an objection answered before it is made: the apostle anticipates and puts himself the charge others would have urged, that he vaunts himself, and this though he had already used so strong a corrective as the question who is sufficient for these things. Chrysostom finds the manner characteristic, since the man is far removed from appearing to say anything great of himself and avoids it even to great superfluity and excess, and he notes the irony that the objection grew out of the apostle's own success in making tribulation look bright and lustrous. Calvin places the accusers more precisely: the complaint came from men grieved to find their own reputation obstructed by his superior excellence, and they had already faulted the earlier letter on the same ground; their pretext was plausible enough, since it is in itself an odious thing to be the trumpeter of one's own praises. Ellicott reconstructs how the report reached him, Titus having told him what was said at Corinth, and lists the passages in the first epistle they had probably seized on. Gill records that some read the sentence without the question mark, as a plain statement, and Wesley takes the subject to be chiefly the apostle himself, though not excluding Timothy, Titus and Silvanus.

The answer turns the demand for credentials into a compliment. Barnes calls it a beautiful and happy turn and sets out why it works: Corinth was a dissolute and abandoned place, a large number there had been converted and a church organised, such an event in such a city would be known abroad, and it had been accomplished under the labour of these men alone. He notes that a few manuscripts and versions read your hearts rather than our, a reading Doddridge adopted, and declines to change the text on that authority. Ellicott and Robertson both hear a play on the two verbs rendered known and read, the same pair used earlier in the letter, and Robertson adds that the thing is literally true, professing Christians being the Bible that other men read. Calvin offers two ways to take the plural, either of Silvanus and Timothy, so that the boast others carry about on paper these carry in men's consciences, or partly of the Corinthians themselves; and he remarks that recommendations obtained by dint of entreaty are often granted by favour rather than by judgement. Robertson reports such letters common in the papyri and lists the instances elsewhere in the New Testament, while Ellicott calls them an important element in the organisation of the early church.

Christ writes and the apostle is only the pen. Calvin puts it flatly, making Christ the author and himself the instrument, so that calumniators may understand it is with Christ they have to do; Clarke breaks the figure into its parts, since Christ dictates, the apostle writes, the hearts of the readers are the substance written on, and the Spirit produces the influence by which the traces are made; Barnes says the same by calling the apostles amanuenses. Henry draws the pastoral point, that there is nothing more delightful to faithful ministers nor more to their commendation than the success of their ministry evidenced in the hearts and lives of those among whom they labour. On the contrasts, Ellicott notes that letters were written on papyrus with a reed and a black pigment, and that the Spirit here takes the place of the older finger of God from the giving of the two tables, the same substitution appearing where one gospel has the finger of God and another the Spirit. He finds three passages behind the phrase about fleshy tables: the heart of flesh promised through Ezekiel, the law written on the heart promised through Jeremiah, and the history of the older covenant itself. Calvin cites the same two prophets.
4:
The confidence expressed at the head of the section is immediately qualified, and the commentators press the qualification hard. Barnes explains that the trust rested not on letters of introduction from men but on the evidence of God's presence in the work, and that every part of it was traced to Christ, the apostle having no success and no hope of success that did not depend on him. Gill fills in what the trust was of, that the converts were living epistles and the ministry had many seals. Ellicott observes that the word sufficient had not been used of himself at all but was the implied answer to the earlier question who is sufficient for these things, and that the Greek has two different prepositions where the English has one, so that a fair paraphrase runs not as though we are sufficient of ourselves to form any estimate as originating with ourselves; the sufficiency flows from God as its source. Robertson draws the same distinction between starting from ourselves and coming out of ourselves, and notes that the noun for sufficiency occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. Wesley reduces the whole to its plainest form: not sufficient so much as to think one good thought, much less to convert sinners.

Barnes argues that the received rendering about able ministers misses the force of the original, since it suggests men of talent inclined to boast, whereas the verb means that God has supplied their deficiency and rendered them competent; he offers the coinage that God has sufficienced them for the work. The note printed with Calvin quotes Barnes at length and then traces where the unhappy word came from, the Latin version's term passing into Wycliffe's rendering made from the Latin, though Erasmus had proposed a different one and Tyndale, in the first translation out of the Greek, wrote made us able to minister; it is Wycliffe's reading that survives in the authorised version. Clarke and Robertson both notice that the verb is built from the same root as the earlier question and so answers it directly. Ellicott presses the missing articles, so that the phrase runs of a new covenant, one not of a written letter but of spirit, and finds a direct reference both to the words spoken at the last supper and to Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant, while the idea of spirit is drawn from Ezekiel. Calvin infers the office's magnitude from the need to be fashioned for it beforehand.

What the letter is makes the chapter's first real crux, and four answers stand. Calvin reports and rejects the oldest, Origen's, that the letter is the grammatical and genuine meaning of Scripture and the spirit its allegorical sense. That exposition, he says, has got into general circulation and become the source of many evils, since it licensed men to adulterate the plain sense, and the more audacity anyone had in doing so the more eminent an interpreter he was accounted, so that the ancients played with the sacred word as if it were a ball to be tossed to and fro, and no frenzy was too monstrous to be brought forward under pretext of allegory. His own reading is that the letter is outward preaching which does not reach the heart and the spirit is living doctrine which makes its way to the soul, the two terms referring not to the exposition of the word but to its influence and fruit. Ellicott takes the letter for the whole written code of Judaism and expressly denies that it means the literal sense as against the mystical. Clarke holds that the old covenant had both its letter and its spirit and that the Jews rested in the former; Henry applies the distinction even to the gospel, since resting in the letter of that leaves a hearer no better.
7:
Chrysostom explains why the argument needed this turn at all: the comparison so far had set stone tables against hearts and a killing letter against a life-giving spirit, but it still wanted the glory of Moses, since nothing in the new covenant was seen with the eyes of the body. That, he says, is exactly what made the old seem great, for its glory was perceived by the senses while the other is perceived by the understanding, and to weaker hearers the superiority of the second is not clear; so the writer, faced with the dulness of his readers, proceeds by placing the difference before them in arguments built out of what he had already said. Ellicott corrects the received rendering of the opening clause, which by using two participles creates a false antithesis between written and engraved and loses the thread: the phrase should run engraved in a writing upon stones, the word for writing being the same as the letter of the previous verse, and the verb should be came into being with glory. He pictures the apostle taking up his Greek version of the law and reproducing its words. Robertson notes that the verb for engraven is used elsewhere of inlaid work on a table sent to Jerusalem by a Ptolemy.

Barnes notices that the expected contrast to the ministration of death would have been the ministration of life, and that the other phrase was chosen instead because the Spirit is the source of life and the title confers a higher dignity; he treats it as the honour of the gospel ministry that this is the means by which the Spirit is imparted. Gill quotes the rabbis on the other side of the comparison, that there is no glory but the law, and grants the law its glories at length before turning them: glorious in its author, in its promulgation amid thunderings and a trumpet, in its matter and in its properties. Clarke concentrates the same admission into an image, that the law was full of splendour and the effulgence rested even on the body of Moses. Ellicott reports that many of the better manuscripts read if there be glory to the ministry of condemnation, and defines the contrasting term as a ministration which has righteousness for its object and result. Wesley alone turns the verse into an argument, asking how the moral law can be a ministration of condemnation if it requires only a sincere obedience proportioned to our infirmity, since on that supposition it would become the ministration of righteousness instead.

Four of them reach independently for the same picture of a lesser light swallowed by a greater. Calvin says that as the moon and stars, though not merely luminous in themselves but spreading light over the whole earth, disappear before the brightness of the sun, so the law however glorious has no glory beside the excellence of the gospel; Barnes writes that its glory was eclipsed as the splendour of moon and stars is by the sun; Robertson says the moon makes a dim light after sunrise and that Christ has thrown Moses into the shade; Wesley reduces it to the sentence that the greater light swallows up the less. Clarke uses the same figure a verse earlier for the glory that was to be absorbed. Ellicott instead reproduces the tense he found in the Greek version of Exodus, so that the clause reads that which had been glorified has not been glorified, and hears behind it the transfiguration, where Moses and Elijah appear in glory and are surpassed. On what precisely is abolished, Gill distinguishes carefully between the matter of the law and its ministry, and between the law in the hands of Moses and in the hands of Christ; Ellicott notes the participle is present, being done away rather than done away.
12:
The inference drawn is a rule for preachers. Henry states it as a duty: ministers ought not, like Moses, to put a veil upon their faces or darken what they should make plain, and they are much to blame if they do not set spiritual things in the clearest light possible, since the gospel is a more clear dispensation and its things are revealed not in types and shadows. Clarke sharpens it into a contrast with the alternatives on offer, that the apostles speak with all imaginable plainness, keeping back nothing, disguising nothing, concealing nothing, and that in this they differ greatly from the Jewish doctors and the Gentile philosophers, who affect obscurity and use figures, metaphors and allegories to hide everything from ordinary people; the apostles, he says, wish that all may hear and speak so that all may understand. Ellicott defines the word itself as the openness which says all, in which there is no reticence or reserve, sets it against the corrupting of the word charged earlier in the letter, and matches it to the claim to have kept back nothing profitable. Barnes takes several hundred words over the sense of hope, canvassing Locke, Rosenmuller and Macknight before settling it.

Why Moses covered his face is answered three ways, and the three do not sit easily together. Barnes observes that Moses never declared his own purpose, and that the account in Exodus suggests the dazzling brightness which made it hard to look at him, a reason the apostle himself seems to allow earlier; yet here another design is intimated, that Moses should be a kind of type and figure of his own dispensation. Ellicott holds that the apostle is following the Greek version of Exodus or an interpretation answering to it, and that on this reading the object was quite different: Moses veiled his face so that they might not see the end, the fading away of a transitory glory, and for them it was as though the brightness were permanent. Calvin refuses the question as put, since the apostle is not reasoning about Moses' intention at all. It was his office to publish the law and there is no doubt he wished its true meaning apprehended by all; he did not deliberately involve his doctrine in obscurity, the fault lay with the people, and being commanded to put a veil between his face and the eyes of the beholders he simply obeyed. Nothing here, Calvin insists, is said to Moses' dishonour.

The veil then changes place. Robertson explains the verb for blinded as meaning to cover with thick skin and so to petrify, and notes that the veil in question is not the identical one but another with the same effect. Barnes prefers hardened for the same reason and points out that the apostle states the fact without assigning its cause. Ellicott presses the grammar: the clause should read that the same veil remains in the reading of the old covenant, the fact not being revealed that the covenant is being done away in Christ, and he objects that referring the words is done away to the veil does violence to a context which applies them throughout to the law itself, especially since a different and appropriate word for withdrawing a veil appears in the next verse. Wesley catches the force of that word, unremoved meaning not so much as folded back to admit a glimmering. On whether a synagogue custom lies behind the image the two disagree flatly: Clarke says there is an evident allusion to the practice of covering the whole head with the tallith at the reading of the law, while Ellicott doubts the usage is old enough and adds that even if it were, the cloth covered head and ears but not the face.
16:
Almost everyone takes the subject of the turning to be Israel, and Calvin alone takes it to be Moses. Barnes refers it to the nation and reads the verse as a promise that the blindness is not permanent, the true sense of their own oracles one day breaking on them with full and irresistible light; Clarke adds that the conversion will be en masse, the whole nation in every place, so that Jew and Gentile make one fold; Gill speaks of the body of the Jewish nation in the latter day looking on him whom they pierced; Wesley says the veil goes that very moment. Ellicott and Robertson both anchor the language in Exodus, where Moses removed the veil whenever he went in to commune with the Lord, Ellicott adding that the very verb for turn is drawn from the same chapter. Calvin objects that the passage has hitherto been badly rendered, since interpreters supply Israel where the apostle is speaking of Moses, that is of the law: the law was turned away in another direction when the Jews shut Christ out of it, and it becomes to them a labyrinth until it is referred to its end. What is said of the law, he adds, applies to all Scripture.

The identification that follows is handled gingerly. Ellicott concedes at once that the words seem at first inconsistent with the formulated precision of the creeds, which make Lord a predicate of the Spirit but would hardly make the Spirit a predicate of the Lord; his answer is that the apostle did not contemplate the language of those later formularies, and that to turn to the Lord Jesus was to turn to one whose essential being, as one with the Father, is Spirit, and who is in one sense the Spirit, the life-giving energy set against the letter that kills. Calvin rejects the metaphysical reading outright: the statement has nothing to do with Christ's essence but points to his office, calling him the spirit of the law, which will be living and life-giving only if he breathes into it, as a body joined to its soul is a living man and without it a useless carcase devoid of feeling. Barnes makes him the sum and substance of the older institutions, in whom the figures and types all centre. Clarke, having taken the word for spirit as the gospel in the earlier verses, keeps that sense here. Robertson prefers Bernard's proposal that Lord bears the sense it has in the Exodus verse being quoted, and warns against pressing the language unduly.

On the liberty they largely agree, and each names a different bondage. Robertson defines it as freedom of access to God without fear, set expressly against the fear of the people in Exodus who were afraid to come near: we need no veil. Clarke reads it as liberty not only from Jewish bondage but from the slavery of sin, from its power, its guilt and its pollution. Wesley lists liberty from servile fear, from guilt, from the power of sin, and liberty to behold the glory with open face, and notes that the veil itself was the emblem of slavery. Calvin uses the same verse to solve a problem he thinks the chapter raises acutely, namely how the praises David heaps on the law, that it converts souls, enlightens the eyes and imparts wisdom to babes, can stand beside the description of a ministry of sin and death; the answer is that the law is one thing when animated and another when left to itself, so that the encomiums belong to it as breathed into by Christ. Gill and Barnes both make the Lord to whom the heart turns the Lord Jesus, Gill noting that without him as its end the law is a mere dead letter.
18:
The first thing several of them establish is who is included. Calvin says he cannot think how it came into the mind of Erasmus to confine to ministers what is evidently common to all believers, and notes that the word for all was added precisely to take in the whole body of the church. Barnes agrees that although the chapter has been mainly about the apostles, this declaration plainly covers all Christians as distinguished from the Jews; Robertson says all of us, not merely ministers; Gill spreads it wider still, every believer whether Jew or Gentile, greater or lesser. On the unveiled face, Ellicott insists the relation to what precedes is sequence and not contrast, and paraphrases: we are free, and so have no need to cover our faces as slaves do before a great king; there is no veil on our hearts and therefore none over the eyes with which we exercise spiritual vision, and we stand as Moses stood before the Lord with the veil withdrawn. Gill distinguishes two things the phrase may cover, the object beheld being unveiled and the beholder being rid of the darkness. Barnes reports Tyndale's rendering, that the Lord's glory appears in us all as in a glass.

The verb behind beholding as in a glass is the chapter's last dispute, and it divides on whether the Christian looks into the mirror or is the mirror. Barnes canvasses the renderings, Macknight's reflecting as mirrors, Doddridge's beholding as by a glass, Locke's with open countenances as mirrors reflecting the glory; he settles on the gospel itself as the burnished metal in which the divine perfections shine and from which they are cast back on the beholder. Calvin allows both senses in Greek usage, quoting the counsel that drunkards and young men should look at themselves in a mirror, but follows the old interpreter in preferring beholding in a mirror. Robertson reports that Philo uses it of beholding as in a mirror, that Plutarch uses the active for reflecting, that Chrysostom takes it the second way, and that either makes good sense. Ellicott is the most careful: the middle voice ordinarily means to look at oneself, which is inapplicable here, but Philo supplies the sense wanted when he makes Moses ask to behold the divine form not mirrored in any created thing but in God himself. So we behold the glory, though not yet face to face, but as mirrored in the person of Christ. Clarke keeps to the reflected light illuminating the face.

On the change itself they converge. Robertson notes that the verb is the one used of the transfiguration and that the tense is continuous, so the point is that we do not lose the glory as Moses did, provided the beholding goes on. Ellicott makes the same identification and adds the parallel about being conformed to the likeness of the Son, drawing the moral that as we gaze the image of the old nature grows less distinct and the new takes its place; he calls the phrase from glory to glory a characteristic way of expressing completeness, and reads it less as passing from stage to stage than as a process which begins in glory and will be consummated in glory. Barnes grounds the mechanism in ordinary experience, that we are moulded by the persons we associate with and the books we read, insensibly taking their sentiments and ways. Clarke says the image lost by the fall is here recovered. Wesley draws the contrast out: Moses saw the glory and his face shone so that he covered it, Israel being unable to bear the reflected light, whereas we behold the glory in the mirror of the word and our faces shine too, yet we do not veil them but diffuse the lustre.
